Day 1
From Hotel: 20 min → Museum of Prehistoric Thera
1.Museum of Prehistoric Thera
Built on the site of a church destroyed in the 1956 earthquake, this Fira museum holds Akrotiri finds — Cycladic figurines, Minoan pottery, gold jewellery, and Bronze Age wall paintings including the ship-procession fresco. The companion piece to Akrotiri, filling in what the buried city no longer shows.

Mitropoleos · Fira
1 min · 2 min → Fira Caldera
2.Fira Caldera
The edge of the caldera in Fira — a sheer 300-metre cliff carved by the eruption — where the island's volcanic origins become fully legible. Whitewashed buildings cascade down terraces toward the submerged crater; the volcanic islands of Nea and Palea Kameni float in the deep-blue water ahead.
Read more
Open 24/7
~1 hr
Caldera Path · Fira
8 min → Imerovigli
3.Imerovigli
The highest caldera-rim village on Santorini, perched 350 m above the submerged crater and offering the island's widest unobstructed caldera view. Imerovigli gave rise to its name — meaning "day watchtower" — from the medieval lookout kept here for pirate sails; Skaros Rock, the remnant of the former island capital, juts below it into the caldera.
Read more
Open 24/7
~1 hr 30 min
Imerovigli · Santorini
10 min → Oia Kasteli Sunset Viewpoint
4.Oia Kasteli Sunset Viewpoint
The ruined Byzantine Kasteli fortress at the northern tip of Oia, facing directly west over the caldera — the most celebrated sunset in the Cyclades. The island of Therasia and the volcanic cone of Nea Kameni frame the drop into the Aegean. Arrive 45 minutes before sunset.

Open 24/7
~2 hr

Day 2
From Hotel: 35 min → Akrotiri Prehistoric City
1.Akrotiri Prehistoric City
The best-preserved Bronze Age settlement in the Aegean, buried by the Theran eruption around 1613 BC. A purpose-built shelter covers multi-storey buildings and narrow stone streets — a Pompeii-like snapshot of Minoan-influenced civilisation frozen in volcanic ash for 3,600 years.

11 min · 3 min → Red Beach
2.Red Beach
A dramatic crescent of deep-red volcanic sand hemmed by sheer ochre and rust-coloured cliffs — the most visually striking beach on the island, shaped by layers of compressed lava and pumice. The water is cold and clear. Rockfall from the cliffs is an active hazard; the coastal path occasionally restricts access.
Read more
Open 24/7
~1 hr
Coastal path may close without notice due to rockfall — beach is accessible by short boat taxi from Akrotiri beach · seasonally
Red Beach · Akrotiri
13 min → Perissa Black Sand Beach
3.Perissa Black Sand Beach
The island's longest black-sand beach, stretching beneath the sheer face of Mesa Vouno on the southeast coast. The sand is coarse volcanic grain from the same Theran eruption that shaped Red Beach — dark and sun-warmed, backed by a long promenade of tavernas and beach bars, with calm, clear water.
Read more
Open 24/7
~1 hr 30 min
Perissa Beach · Perissa
12 min → Ancient Thira
4.Ancient Thira
A Dorian city founded in the 9th century BC on the 396-metre summit of Mesa Vouno, between Kamari and Perissa. Excavations begun in 1896 uncovered an agora, temples to Apollo Karneios, a theatre, and a stone road network spanning the Hellenistic and Roman periods.

Day 3
From Hotel: 20 min · 6 min → Amoudi Bay
1.Amoudi Bay
A small working harbour tucked into the volcanic cliffs directly below Oia, reached by roughly 300 stone steps. Fishing boats and a handful of seafood tavernas line the base of the caldera wall — a sea-level counterpoint to Oia's clifftop views, and a well-known sunset spot in its own right.
Read more
Open 24/7
~1 hr
Reached only via roughly 300 steps from Oia — no vehicle access
Amoudi Bay · Oia
20 min → Skaros Rock
2.Skaros Rock
A sheer volcanic promontory jutting from the caldera rim below Imerovigli, once crowned by a 13th-century Venetian fortress that served as the island's capital until eruptions collapsed it into the sea. A short cliffside path leads out past the Theoskepasti chapel to open caldera views on three sides.
Read more
Open 24/7
~1 hr 30 min
Agios Georgios · Imerovigli
25 min → Emporio Kasteli
3.Emporio Kasteli
A still-inhabited fortified village built around 1450 at the foot of Profitis Ilias — the largest of Santorini's five kastelia. Tightly packed houses form the outer fortress wall; the square Goulas watchtower at the northern edge is the best preserved on the island.

Day 4
From Hotel: 25 min → Pyrgos Kallistis
1.Pyrgos Kallistis
Santorini's former capital, built amphitheatrically on the island's highest hill. Narrow labyrinthine streets climb through a fortified medieval settlement to the ruined Venetian Kasteli at the summit — the best-preserved of the island's five castle villages, and one of the few left largely untouched by tourism.
Read more
Open 24/7
~1 hr
Kasteli · Pyrgos
10 min → Megalochori
2.Megalochori
The most intact of Santorini's winemaking villages, built above a network of kafiria — cave cellars carved into the volcanic pumice — where barrels and amphorae have aged wine for centuries. The arcaded Venetian square at the village centre dates to the 17th century; the surrounding lanes are lined with the distinctive earth-coloured mansions of the island's merchant wine families.
Read more
Open 24/7
~1 hr
Megalochori · Santorini
35 min · 7 min → Santo Wines
3.Santo Wines
The island's largest wine cooperative, perched on the caldera cliff between Pyrgos and Fira with a terrace looking over the submerged volcano and the islands of Nea and Palea Kameni. Founded in 1947 and drawing grapes from over 1,200 member growers, Santo produces Santorini's two signature wines: dry mineral Assyrtiko from ancient ungrafted vines, and Vinsanto, a sun-dried sweet wine aged in oak.
Daily 10:00am - 10:00pm

Episkopi Gonia · Pyrgos
13 min → Kamari Beach
4.Kamari Beach
The longest black-sand beach on Santorini, backed by the sheer 400-metre cliff face of Mesa Vouno — the same rock that carries Ancient Thira above. The sand is not black but a dark volcanic gravel that grows hot in the afternoon sun; a broad promenade runs the full length behind the loungers, lined with cafés, seafood restaurants, and the island's only open-air cinema.

Day 5
From Hotel: 27 min · 40 min → Nea Kameni
1.Nea Kameni
The newest island in the Aegean, formed entirely by eruptions since 1707 and still volcanically active. A path from the boat landing leads to the main crater — yellow sulphur deposits line the rim, and on clear days the caldera walls of Santorini and Thirasia form the full horizon. The island last erupted in 1950 and remains classified as active.
Read more
Open 24/7
~1 hr 30 min
Reached only by boat from Fira Old Port — tickets sold at the port or in advance via tour operators
Nea Kameni · Santorini Caldera
20 min → Palea Kameni Hot Springs
2.Palea Kameni Hot Springs
A patch of thermal water rising from the volcanic rock on Palea Kameni's western shore — the spring stains the sea iron-rust orange and warms it noticeably for several metres around the swim zone. Swimmers reach it by jumping from the boat; the site has been documented since antiquity, directly above a hydrothermal vent from the same magma chamber as Nea Kameni.
Read more
Open 24/7
~45 min
No beach or jetty — swim directly from the boat; included in all volcano boat excursions from Fira Old Port
Palea Kameni · Santorini Caldera
40 min → Fira Old Port · 20 min → Firostefani
3.Firostefani
A caldera-rim neighbourhood between Fira and Imerovigli at the midpoint of the island's caldera path. Whitewashed chapels and cave houses perch above the 300-metre drop to the water; the westward view is fully open — no ridge, no promontory, no bell towers — sweeping across to Nea Kameni, Thirasia, and the volcanic rim of Oia.

Local Tastes
Tomatokeftedes
Santorini's signature tomato fritters — the island's cherry tomatoes grown in volcanic soil · mixed with onion · mint · and flour into small crisp cakes. Intensely flavoured and found on nearly every Fira restaurant menu.
Ouzeri· Stani Tavern
Santorini Fava
A PDO puree of yellow split peas grown in Santorini's volcanic soil since ancient times — silkier and more intensely flavoured than mainland fava · served warm with capers and a drizzle of olive oil.
Ouzeri
White Eggplant
A pale-skinned eggplant variety cultivated only on Santorini — smaller · sweeter · and less bitter than conventional eggplant · eaten baked · grilled · or in salad. Rarely found off the island.
Stani Tavern
Assyrtiko Wine
The indigenous white grape of Santorini · grown in basket-woven vines trained low on the volcanic soil — produces a dry · mineral · high-acid white that is among the most distinctive wines in Greece. Best tasted at source.
Santo Wines· Venetsanos Winery
Vinsanto
A naturally sweet amber wine from sun-dried Assyrtiko grapes — intensely concentrated with apricot and honey notes · aged for years in oak barrels. A PDO product and the island's only dessert wine.
Santo Wines

Getting Around
Uber
Foreign number: accepted.
Operates on Santorini during the summer season. Fares are higher than on the mainland and wait times can be long; most practical for the late-evening run from Oia back to Fira.

Heads Up
Red Beach — Rockfall Closures
The coastal path to Red Beach closes without notice when rockfall from the volcanic cliffs is assessed as a hazard.
Oia Sunset — Kasteli Crowds
The Kasteli viewpoint fills 45-60 minutes before sunset in peak season. Latecomers face blocked sightlines or standing positions on the path.
Akrotiri — Reduced Hours Monday · Thursday
The excavation closes at 3:30pm on Mondays and Thursdays instead of the standard 8:00pm. Visiting in the afternoon on these days will fail.
Worth Knowing

Everything is the Eruption

Almost everything that makes Santorini singular traces back to a single event: the Theran eruption around 1613 BC, one of the largest volcanic explosions in the last 10,000 years. The caldera you look across is the collapsed throat of the volcano. The sheer cliffs the hotels cling to are the eruption's interior wall. The red and black beaches are compressed lava. The whitewashed villages perch on pumice.

Even the wine is the eruption. Santorini's volcanic soil is so nutrient-poor and porous that the Assyrtiko vine has to push its roots metres deep to find moisture — producing a grape of extraordinary mineral concentration that no other terroir in Greece can replicate. The basket-vine training, the white cubes against the caldera, the blue domes, the sunset crowds at Kasteli: they are all just people arranging themselves around the aftermath of a catastrophe.
